Micro-aerated fermentation enhances acetate production from high-rate 
activated sludge to supply carbon source for heterotrophic denitratation

A B S T R A C T   
Heterotrophic denitratation coupled with anammox is a high-efficiency and low-cost process to scavenge residual 
nitrate and ammonium from the mainstream partial nitritation/anammox process. Fermentate derived from the 
carbon-concentrated sludge, e.g., chemically enhanced high-rate activated sludge (CEHRAS), is a valuable car­
bon source for heterotrophic denitratation. However, acetate rather than all volatile fatty acids (VFAs) in the 
fermentate results in high nitrite accumulation. Micro-aeration may be a promising technology to facilitate VFA 
production and acetate proportion. This study implemented performance comparison and mechanism analyses 
on two different micro-aeration modes (i.e., continuous and intermittent micro-aeration) of CEHRAS anaerobic 
fermentation. Batch fermentation tests showed that the low-intensity micro-aeration (4.62 mL/(L⋅min)) 
increased 2.2 times of VFA productions compared with unaerated blank. Higher oxygen dosages (7.69 and 15.4 
mL/(L⋅min)) increased acetate proportion though reduced VFA production, largely due to the elimination of 
hydrogen inhibition in acetogenesis and the facultative consumption strengthen. Further, the intermittent micro- 
aeration effectively limits the aerobic respiration in the later stage. Moreover, model substrate tests elucidated 
that micro-aeration accelerated all steps of protein degradation. The long-term beneficial effects of micro- 
aeration on VFA production (104 vs. 54.3 mg COD/g VSS) and acetate ratio (59.0% vs. 41.0%) were vali­
dated by operating sequencing batch reactors with and without micro-aeration, respectively. Additionally, 
micro-aeration enriched essential functional microorganisms rather than regulated microbial diversity. Model 
simulations revealed the crucial roles of increasing acetate proportion in fermentate. The intercellular storage 
process had higher rate constant and substrate affinity based on acetate than other VFAs, which was the main 
reason for the higher nitrite accumulation of acetate. Thereby, micro-aeration fermentate from CEHRAS is an 
ideal carbon source in heterotrophic denitratation.   
1. Introduction 
In the recent decade, high-rate activated sludge (HRAS) process for 
carbon capture and anammox-based process for low-cost nitrogen 
removal are gradually regarded as crucial processes of future water 
resource recovery factories (WRRFs) [1–3]. In a regular HRAS reactor, 
the carbon capture efficiency is usually limited by collision efficiency, 
floc formation, and floc strength. The addition of iron salts could 
improve these limitation factors, increasing carbon capture efficiency. 
Moreover, the removal of phosphorus could be enhanced by chemical 
precipitation [4]. The formed iron-phosphate compounds can be further 
recovered as vivianite, which gradually becomes a hot recovered type of 
phosphorus source in recent years [5–7]. The chemically (iron salt) 
enhanced high-rate activated sludge (CEHRAS) process has the potential 
to become a more popular carbon capture process than the regular HRAS 
process in future. Compared with the traditional nitrification/denitrifi­
cation process, the partial nitritation/anammox (PNA) process has many 
advantages, such as saving ~60% oxygen and 100% organic demands 
and reducing ~90% sludge production [8,9]. However, the theoretical 
maximum nitrogen removal of PNA is limited to 89% due to the oxi­
dization of nitrite to nitrate by the nitrite:nitrate oxidoreductase on 
anammoxosome [10]. Meanwhile, the possible low ratio of alkalinity to

ammonium could limit the conversion of ammonium to nitrite in the PN 
process, resulting in a lower nitrite to ammonium ratio than that of 
theory and high concentration of residual ammonium in the effluent 
[11]. Moreover, the complete suppression of nitrite-oxidizing bacteria 
(NOB) is difficult in practice [12]. In these cases, the effluent total ni­
trogen (TN) concentration of PNA is hard to meet the gradually strict 
discharge standards, especially treating high ammonium concentration 
of wastewater, such as toilet wastewater (blackwater) and anaerobically 
digested sludge liquor. 
Heterotrophic denitratation, the reduction of nitrate to nitrite with 
organics as electron donor, is an effective remedy to the problem of high- 
concentration inorganic nitrogen in PNA effluent. By heterotrophic 
denitratation, the nitrate formed in the anammox reaction could be 
reduced to nitrite, which could be reused by anammox bacteria to 
convert the residual ammonium to dinitrogen [13–16]. Thus, most of the 
residual nitrate and ammonium could be removed. However, after car­
bon capture by CEHRAS process and aerobic oxidation by the partial 
nitritation process, there is little organic source in mainstream for het­
erotrophic denitratation [4]. Anaerobic fermentation is a promising 
technology to recover the carbon source captured and concentrated in 
CEHRAS. The produced volatile fatty acids (VFAs) can serve as the 
organic source for heterotrophic denitratation. However, not all VFA 
components perform well in terms of nitrite accumulation [17–19]. As 
the carbon source, acetate can result in a higher nitrite accumulation 
ratio than other VFA components and is usually adopted in lab-scale and 
pilot-scale reactors of heterotrophic denitratation [12,20–22]. There­
fore, it is of great significance to increase acetate production and pro­
portion of the fermentation of CEHRAS. 
Some advanced oxidizing agents, such as potassium permanganate 
[23], peroxymonosulfate (PMS) [24], potassium ferrate [25,26], 
hydrogen peroxide [27], calcium hypochlorite [28], and calcium 
peroxide [29,30], were found conducive to the transformations of other 
VFAs to acetate. Zhang et al. [28] found that the reactive oxygen species 
(mainly ⋅OH) induced by Ca(ClO)2 (0 vs. 0.05 g/g TSS) might contribute 
to the improvement of acetate proportion (30.6% vs. 46.3%). Li et al. 
[29] demonstrated that the ratio of acetic acid was enhanced from 
45.1% to 60.2% with CaO2 addition increasing from 0 to 0.2 g/g VSS, 
while Ca(OH)2 had no obvious effect on the ratio of acetate, and 
assumed that this phenomenon might be attributed to the chemical 
oxidation of CaO2 (⋅O2
– and ⋅OH) or functional microbe change, i.e., the 
increasing population of Firmicutes. Yang et al. [24] and Xu et al. [23] 
reported that the PMS and KMnO4 addition facilitated the acetate pro­
duction and the removal of larger-molecule VFAs, respectively. The 
behind mechanisms were both that all the bioprocesses and enzymes 
relevant to anaerobic fermentation were inhibited in the presence of 
powerful oxidants (PMS and KMnO4), but the suppression to methano­
genesis and F420 were much severer than that to others, such as ace­
togenesis process and acetate kinase. It is probable that the inhibition 
effects on all bioprocesses increase the fermentation period or reactor 
size. Moreover, the addition of chemicals has other obvious disadvan­
tages, such as the high dosage increasing operating costs and the 
chemical wastes production, and the oxidative property increasing the 
risks of transportation, preservation, and use. 
Compared to the above-mentioned chemicals, oxygen is a more 
environmental-friendly oxidant, which widely exists in the atmosphere 
with a high proportion. Recently, micro-aeration, supplying a small 
amount of pure oxygen gas or air, has been considered a cheaper green 
substitute for the dosing of advanced oxidizing agents. Although the aim 
of micro-aeration in most literature is to decrease VFA accumulation and 
increase CH4 production of anaerobic digestion [31–34], the mecha­
nisms behind micro-aeration assisting anaerobic digestion can be used to 
increase the acetate production and proportion of anaerobic fermenta­
tion. The underlying rationales are as follows: (1) oxygen is an electron 
acceptor of facultative microbes and can augment their activity and 
diversity [35,36]; (2) the reactive oxygen species stimulated by oxygen 
can degrade the phospholipid membrane, DNA, and protein [37,38]; (3) 
the hydrogenotrophic methanogens can converse the CO2 produced 
from the aerobic oxidation of VFA to methane [32]; (4) the co-existence 
interaction between microorganisms can be established, for instance, 
producing anti-oxidative enzymes and protecting inner oxygen-sensitive 
anaerobes (e.g., methanogens), however, over-dose oxygen beyond the 
oxygen consumption capacity of facultative microorganisms would 
break this aerotolerant mechanism [39]. The first two mechanisms were 
conducive to the hydrolysis and acidogenesis processes of anaerobic 
fermentation. The third mechanism indicates that oxygen can enhance 
the aerobic oxidation of VFAs by the aerobic respiration of facultative 
microorganisms. The fourth mechanism implies that the conversion of 
acetate to CH4 could be suppressed under higher-dose oxygen condi­
tions. Thus, micro-aeration is a switching tool among the multiple 
purposes for the anaerobic processes. Yu et al. [40] proposed that the 
low-dose aeration (5 mg O2/L/Cycle) indeed enhanced the hydrolysis 
efficiency (34.7% vs. 48.7%) and methane yield of blackwater (39.6% 
vs. 50.7%), while the VFA accumulation sharply increased and the 
methane yield simultaneously declined at higher oxygen dosages (50 
and 150 mg O2/L/Cycle). The medium-dose aeration (50 mg O2/L/ 
Cycle) obtained maximum VFA accumulation. Sawatdeenarunat et al. 
[41] reported that the positive effects of micro-aeration on anaerobic 
digestion of lignocellulosic biomass, and also found VFAs yield showed a 
quadratic correlation with oxygen dosage. 
Based on the above literature review and further analyses, micro- 
aeration is considered a promising and feasible method for improving 
CEHRAS anaerobic fermentation, especially in enhancing acetate pro­
duction. However, several vital problems are worth to be clarified: (1) 
which is the better micro-aeration mode, continuous or intermittent 
micro-aeration? (2) the effects of micro-aeration on each process in 
anaerobic fermentation are unclear until now; (3) the performance of 
micro-aerated fermentate derived from CEHRAS as a carbon source for 
the heterotrophic denitratation has not been verified. 
To our best knowledge, this study is the first report to use micro- 
aeration to increase the acetate production and proportion of anaer­
obic fermentation with CEHRAS as substrates. This study compared the 
performance of the continuous and intermittent micro-aeration strate­
gies. Batch fermentation experiments investigated the influences of 
aeration intensity and aeration cycle time and then explored the 
enhancement mechanism of acetate production by model substrate ex­
periments. Further, sequencing batch reactors with or without micro- 
aeration fed with actual CEHRAS were carried out to validate the 
long-term effects of micro-aeration on VFA production and distribution. 
Then, batch denitrification experiments verified the high nitrite accu­
mulation performance of micro-aerated fermentate. Finally, the in­
fluences of carbon/nitrogen ratio, acetate proportion in fermentate, and 
process parameters on heterotrophic denitratation were predicted by 
modeling. 
2. Method and material 
2.1. Source of CEHRAS 
The sludge for fermentation was collected from a lab-scale CEHRAS 
sequencing batch reactor (SBR) with a working volume of 4 L. The 
CEHRAS SBR was fed on real blackwater collected from a maintenance 
hole connecting toilets of one campus library and two teaching buildings 
on the Siping Campus of Tongji University, Shanghai City, China. 
Characteristics of the real blackwater were summarized in our pervious 
study [11]. The total sludge retention time (SRT) and aerobic hydraulic 
retention time (HRT) of CEHRAS SBR were 0.25 ~ 0.5 days and 30 min, 
respectively. In order to enhance the flocculation process, a total of 60 
mg FeCl3 (calculated as Fe) was added with 2 L influent of real black­
water. The CEHRAS was thickened and stored in a refrigerator at 4 ℃. 
The solid concentration of the thickened CEHRAS was 10 ~ 15 g VSS/L. 
Before use, the CEHRAS in different storage buckets was mixed into a 
container and diluted to 9.0 g VSS/L.

2.2. Lab-scale fermentation reactor 
The lab-scale fermentation reactor was a double-layer glass vessel 
with a working volume of 1.0 ~ 1.5 L (Fig. 1). The out layer was a water 
bath that could exchange heat with a self-made thermostat (a module of 
four semiconductor chilling plates (CL-C067, Heke Tech, China)), which 
could be switched between heating and cooling states by exchanging 
their positive and negative poles connecting power supply. The reaction 
liquid in the inner layer was mixed by a 50 W overhead stirrer (LC-OES- 
60SH, LICHEN, China). Compressed gas (nitrogen gas or air) was 
injected into the reaction liquid bottom by a stainless ring sparger with 
evenly distributed holes. The gas flowrates were manually regulated by 
rotor flowmeters. The fermentation reactor was air-tight. However, the 
injected gas could leave the reactor by a one-way valve. The fermenta­
tion reactor equipped with a pH sensor (SIN-PH-5015, LONTROL, 
China) and an oxidation–reduction potential (ORP) sensor (LONTROL, 
China). The pH sensor also detected temperature (T). The pH, ORP and T 
signals were logged by the self-made control system. The control system 
equipped with an S7-200 smart programmable logical controller (PLC) 
(SIEMENS, Germany). The pH and T of reaction liquid and aeration 
frequency were automatically controlled by the control system. Ac­
cording to the buffer capacity of reaction liquid, different concentration 
of HCl (0.2 ~ 2 mol/L) and NaOH (0.2 ~ 2 mol/L) solutions were pre­
pared for pH control. 
All the batch fermentation and denitrification experiments and the 
long-term fermentation experiments could be executed in the lab-scale 
fermentation reactors. Four lab-scale fermentation reactors were used 
in this study. 
2.3. Batch fermentation experiments of continuous micro-aeration 
Firstly, 1.3 L CEHRAS was filled into a lab-scale fermentation 
reactor, and the CEHRAS was stirred at 200 rpm. Then, compressed 
nitrogen gas (1 L/min) was injected for 10 min to strip potential dis­
solved oxygen (DO). Next, pH and T controls were started. When pH and 
T values reached their corresponding setpoints (pH = 8.0, T = 25 ℃, 
respectively), continuous micro-aeration was executed: Compressed air 
was continuously supplied to the fermentation reactor until the batch 
experiment was over (one week usually). The pH was set closely to the 
actual pH of the original CEHRAS, mainly for decreasing the addition 
amounts of chemical reagents as far as possible. Four micro-aeration 
intensities were set: 0 (control), 4.62, 7.69, and 15.4 mL air per min­
ute per liter sludge (mL/(L⋅min)). Every 0.5 ~ 2 days, 20 mL sample was 
grabbed using a syringe. One 10 mL sample was immediately centri­
fuged at 4000 rpm for 5 min. Then, the supernatant was filtrated by 0.45 
μm polyethersulfone (PES) filters. The filtrate and another 10 mL sample 
were immediately stored at 4 ℃ waiting for analyses. 
2.4. Batch fermentation experiments of intermittent micro-aeration 
The basic procedures of batch fermentation experiments with inter­
mittent micro-aeration were the same as those with continuous micro- 
aeration. The difference was that the compressed air supply of the 
intermittent micro-aeration was periodically switched on and switched 
off during the fermentation period. One intermittent aeration cycle was 
comprised of an aeration phase (air supply on) and a non-aeration phase 
(air supply off). In this study, the total cycle time was fixed at 60 min, 
while the aeration cycle time was adjusted for different experimental 
groups. Three aeration cycle times were implemented, i.e., 15 min, 30 
min, and 45 min. The micro-aeration intensity during the aeration phase 
was controlled at 7.69 mL/(L⋅min) in experimental groups. The 
continuous micro-aeration batch with 7.69 mL/(L⋅min) in section 2.3 
was regarded as the control group, which could be considered as 
intermittent aeration with 60 min of aeration phase cycle time. The “15 
min/60 min”, “30 min/60 min”, “45 min/60 min”, and the “60 min/60 
min” were used to represent the above experimental and control groups 
in the following text in brief. 
2.5. Long-term operation of intermittent micro-aeration fermentation 
One lab-scale fermentation reactor (section 2.2) worked with 
sequencing batch procedure was implemented to assess the long-term 
operation performance of CEHRAS fermentation with intermittent 
micro-aeration assistant. Intermittent aeration was conducted during

this reactor. The total intermittent aeration cycle was 60 min with an 
aeration cycle of 45 min. The mixed liquid volume was 1.3 L, while the

AnSBR (SRT = 2 days) and MaSBR (SRT = 5 days) were 15 days and 30 
days, respectively. The pH and T of both reactors were controlled at 8.0 
and 25.0 ℃, respectively. 
2.6. Influences of micro-aeration on hydrolysis and acidification in 
anaerobic fermentation 
Anaerobic fermentation of sludge generally contained several basic 
steps, i.e., hydrolysis, acidogenesis, acetogenesis, and these steps 
directly affect the eventually VFA production. Thus, it is essential to 
assess the role of micro-aeration on each step involved in anaerobic 
fermentation. However, these steps generally co-occur in actual sludge 
fermentation, for instance, the soluble chemical oxygen demand (sCOD), 
soluble protein, soluble carbohydrate and three-dimensional excitation 
emission matrix (3D-EEM) on 2 d only reflect the comprehensive effect 
of solubilization and hydrolysis. Herein, the batch experiments of in­
fluence of micro-aeration intensity (0 ~ 15.4 mL/(L⋅min)) on above 
processes were performed with model substrates. 
Hydrolysis tests: 1 g/L dextran (model carbohydrate), 2 g/L bovine 
serum albumin (BSA, model protein) and inoculum were added in the 
synthetic wastewater. The synthetic wastewater compositions were ac­
cording to Wang et al. [42]. Because CEHARS also contains high con­
centration of substrate with low biological activity, the inoculum was a 
little of wasted activated sludge (WAS), which was aerated overnight to 
remove unused substrate. In addition, the aeration system was start up 
when ORP of the fermentation systems was lower than −200 ~ −150 
mV for preventing the direct oxidation of model substrates in initial 
periods. The hydrolysis degree was evaluated by the degradation rate of 
dextran and BSA after 3 days. 
Acidification tests: all operations were the same as Hydrolysis Test 
except that the model substrates were replaced with 1 g/L glucose 
(model monosaccharide) and 2 g/L L-glutamate (model amino acid). 
The acidification degree was evaluated by the degradation rate of 
glucose and L-glutamate after 3 days. 
2.7. Denitrification batch experiments 
All denitrification batch experiments were performed in a lab-scale 
fermentation reactor with a working volume of 1.5 L (section 2.2). 
Additional DO sensor (COS22D, Endress + Hauser, Germany) was used 
to monitor DO in the bulk. The sludge for denitrification tests was taken 
from the membrane tank of a municipal wastewater treatment plant 
(WWTP) located in Hangzhou City, China. The sludge was washed three 
times to decrease residual substrate concentration, and the sludge con­
centration was finally all diluted to 2.5 g VSS/L in the reactor. Mean­
while, 2.8 mL macro-element stock solution and 0.42 mL trace-element 
stock solution was added into the reactor [43]. The T and pH were both 
controlled at the optimal denitratation conditions (pH = 8.5 ± 0.1, T =
25.0 ± 0.1 ℃, see in Fig. S1 and Fig. S2), and the reactor was stirred at 
200 rpm. The sludge mixed liquid was purged with nitrogen gas until the 
DO was lower than 0.05 mg/L. 
While pH, T, and DO reached and ensured stable initial conditions, 
NO3-N stock solution (25 mg N/mL) was added into the reactor to 
achieve the initial NO3-N concentration of 30 mg N/L. Then, different 
carbon source was added, resulting in an initial COD/NO3-N ratio of 3.0 
or 6.0 mg COD/mg N. The carbon sources were sodium acetate solution 
(170 mg COD/mL), synthetic fermentates with the different acetate 
proportion (0%, 20%, 40%, 60%, 70%, 80%, and 100%) and real micro- 
aeration fermentate from the MaSBR. During the 240 min batch period, 
10 mL sample was grabbed with a syringe every 20 ~ 30 min. The 
sample was injected into a 15 mL centrifuge tube, and 20 μL chloroform 
was added to completely inhibit biological activity. Concentrated HCl 
and H2SO4 were not recommended, because they caused significant 
interference on chemical analysis. The sample was immediately centri­
fuged at 4000 rpm and then filtered with 0.45 μm PES filters. The filtrate 
was stored at 4 ℃ before use. 
2.8. The establishment of dual-substrate and two-step denitrification 
model 
The dual-substrate and two-step denitrification (DSTSD) model is a 
simplified modification of the Activated Sludge Model 3 (ASM3). The 
DSTSD model consists of five components and six transformation pro­
cesses. The dual substrates are acetate (SAc) and non-acetate VFAs 
(SNAc). The two-step denitrification means that nitrate (SNO3) and nitrite 
(SNO2) are separately considered. In the DSTSD model, only anoxic 
storage and growth processes of denitrifiers were considered. The pro­
cesses and their kinetic rate expressions are listed in Table S1. The 
stoichiometric and composition matrix is shown in Table S2. 
2.9. Analytical methods and statistical analysis 
The procedures of DNA extraction and 16S rRNA gene high- 
throughput sequencing and analytic methods of chemical and physical 
composition are detailed in the Supporting Information. The difference 
between a group of data and a reference value was compared by one- 
sample t-test. The difference between two groups of data was 
compared by two-sample t-test. For two-sample t-test, if the variance 
was not equal, Welch correction was used. Correlation coefficients were 
calculated by Pearson method. All the statistical analyses were con­
ducted on the platform of OriginPro 2018. 
3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Influences of aeration intensity on CEHRAS anaerobic fermentation 
with continuous micro-aeration 
3.1.1. VFAs production and compositions 
Figure 2(a) presents the productions of VFAs during seven-day 
anaerobic fermentation with and without continuous micro-aeration. 
Obviously, the VFA production of high-rate activated sludge was 
enhanced by continuous micro-aeration, of which efficacy was depen­
dent on the aeration intensity. The VFA production of the unaerated 
batch reached the maximum at 40 h, but those of the aerated batches 
still showed a considerable increase thereafter. The maximum VFA 
productions were 113, 97.6, and 73.8 mg COD/g VSS, respectively, 
which were 2.2, 1.9, and 1.5 times higher than that of the unaerated 
blank (i.e., 50.6 mg COD/g VSS), respectively, when the aeration in­
tensities were 4.62 mL/(L⋅min), 7.69 mL/(L⋅min) and 15.4 mL/(L⋅min), 
respectively. Wang et al. [44] also reported that the maximum VFAs 
production enhanced by 54.3% after micro-oxygen bio-pretreatment 
with oilseed rape straw as substrate. It suggests that a trace injection of 
oxygen probably promote the propagation of facultative anaerobes and 
the synthesis of extracellular hydrolases, consequently accelerating hy­
drolysis and acidogenesis processes. The decreasing trend of the 
maximum VFA production with increased micro-aeration intensity 
might be due to the enhancement of aerobic respiration by facultative 
microorganisms [39]. In addition, the VFAs did not decrease in the later 
stage of the unaerated batch, indicating that the absence of methano­
genesis process due to the short SRT (0.5 days) of high-rate activated 
sludge, which is accordant with scarcely methane in gas composition 
detection of all groups. The non-existence of methanogens (see in

hydrogen could be utilized as the electron donor by some microorgan­

process [32]. In addition, the hydrogen might be expelled from the 
fermenter by the air supply, which would play a significant role in 
reducing the hydrogen pressure. 
Notably, the VFA distribution greatly influences the downstream 
application of VFAs. It is known that acetate and propionate were the 
suitable carbon source in terms of the traditional denitrification [46]. As 
for the heterotrophic denitratation process, acetate caused higher nitrite 
accumulation performance compared to other VFAs [12]. Rijn et al. [19] 
found that longer-chain VFAs (such as butyrate and valerate) did not 
present obvious nitrite accumulation, mainly owing to the tendency of 
donating electrons to nitrite reductase. Ali et al. [16] observed the nitrite 
accumulation ratio (NAR) of ＞80% using pure acetate as a carbon 
source in long-term pilot operation, whereas only 49% was achieved 
with primary sludge fermentate (50% acetate proportion). Thereby, 
high proportion acetate of fermentate from CEHRAS would be a 
preferred substitute carbon source in the heterotrophic denitratation 
system. 
3.1.2. Influences of micro-aeration on solubilization, hydrolysis, 
acidogenesis and acetogenesis processes 
The concentrations of soluble proteins, soluble carbohydrates and 
sCOD after two-day micro-aeration fermentation were measured to 
evaluate the solubilization and hydrolysis processes of CEHRAS. As 
presented in Fig. 3(a), there were no large differences in the soluble 
carbohydrates among different batches. The concentrations of soluble 
carbohydrates were respectively 31.9, 43.4, 41.5, and 35.5 mg/L in 
batches with aeration intensity of 0, 4.62, 7.69, and 15.4 mL/(L⋅min), 
respectively. In contrast, the contents of released proteins were obvi­
ously higher than that of carbohydrates, and the variation trend of 
which was consistent with VFA productions among different levels of 
micro-aeration intensity. The concentrations of soluble proteins were 
172, 145, and 122 mg/L, respectively, when the micro-aeration in­
tensities were controlled at 4.62, 7.69, and 15.4 mL/(L⋅min), respec­
tively, much higher than that of the unaerated batch (i.e., 93.9 mg/L). 
There are two possible reasons for the similar contents of soluble car­
bohydrates in Fig. 3(a). First, the hydrolysis and acidification of car­
bohydrates were rapid and unrelated to the aeration intensity basically 
(see Fig. 3(g), (h)). In this case, the released carbohydrates and the 
corresponding hydrolyzed products (i.e., oligosaccharides) could be 
readily consumed. Second, the contents of carbohydrates in CEHRAS 
were much lower than proteins. Moreover, the above results imply that 
the impacts of micro-aeration intensity on hydrolysis and acidification 
of proteins play a decisive role in VFA production. Apparently, the sol­
ubilization performance was dramatically improved with the presence 
of micro-aeration, which was also reported by Lim and Wang [31], and 
then the considerable released macromolecular proteins would be 
degraded in the hydrolysis. Extensive studies have illustrated that the 
beneficial effects of micro-aeration treatment on hydrolysis process 
[31,40,47–49], and the hydrolysis rate might be positively correlated 
with the oxygen injection amount. Therefore, in the range of 4.62 ~ 
15.4 mL/(L⋅min), the soluble protein decreased with the increased 
aeration intensity (Pearson correlation coefficient = -0.958). Mean­
while, the aerobic respiration by facultative bacteria could be 
strengthened with the increased oxygen injection amount. In this case, 
more amino acids would be converted to CO2 and H2O rather than VFA. 
Accordingly, VFA, sCOD, and soluble protein decreased simultaneously 
at higher aeration intensity in Fig. 2(a), Fig. 3(a) and (b). 
The EEM fluorescence spectrum was employed for further charac­
terizing dissolved organic matters (DOMs) in supernatants of the micro- 
aerated and unaerated batches. Two protein-like substance peaks were 
observed in the EEM fluorescence spectrum, i.e., peak A (Ex/Em 270/ 
300) and peak B (Ex/Em 275/350), which were associated with tyrosine 
and tryptophan protein-like substances, respectively. Peak C ((Ex/Em ＞ 
280/＞380) was related to the humic acid-like organics [50–52]. 
The intensities of peak A and peak B in the fermenter with micro- 
aeration treatment were greater than those of the unaerated batch. 
However, peak A and peak B gradually became weak as the aeration 
intensity increased. It could be inferred that micro-aeration can accel­
erate the release of DOMs (mainly are tryptophan and tyrosine protein- 
like substances). Nevertheless, if the micro-aeration intensity is too high, 
the hydrolysis rate of protein might be sped up, and then remarkable 
amino acids tend to be utilized by the aerobic respiration of heterotro­
phic bacteria, which was consistent with the results inferred from pro­
teins variation in Fig. 3(a). Additionally, compared to the unaerated 
batch, peak C attributed to the humic acid-like organics only appeared in 
the three micro-aerated batches. More specially, the intensities of peak C 
in the fermenter with high micro-aeration intensities (7.69 and 15.4 mL/ 
(L⋅min)) were lower than that of the low micro-aeration intensity (4.62 
mL/(L⋅min)). It indicates that the massive humic acid-like organics 
released to the supernatant with the accelerate of sludge disintegration 
triggered by micro-aeration. Previous studies confirmed that recalci­
trant organics could be partially degraded to biodegradable substrates 
after PMS or KMnO4 addition. It was reported that KMnO4 could destroy 
organics containing C = C bonds or electron-rich moieties, while the 
PMS could scavenge conduction band electrons and form sulfate radical 
[23,24]. Furthermore, the amounts of intracellular enzymes (e.g., 
monooxygenase and peroxidase) are abundantly secreted in the pres­
ence of limited aeration, causing the activation and structure change of 
refractory organics [38,53]. Similarly, part of recalcitrant organics could 
be degraded and used under micro-aeration condition, which might 
provide more biodegradable organics for VFA generation. However, the 
biodegradable organics derived from the humic acid-like organics were 
mostly used by aerobic respiration rather than anaerobic fermentation 
with higher micro-aeration intensities (7.69 and 15.4 mL/(L⋅min)), ac­
cording to the decreased VFAs in the later stage of the fermentation 
period. 
From the above results, the micro-aeration participation is effective 
in enhancing CEHRAS disintegration and VFAs production. The anaer­
obic fermentation of CEHRAS containing several bioprocesses, i.e., hy­
drolysis, acidogenesis, acetogenesis, more importantly, the VFA- 
consumption steps (aerobic respiration by facultative anaerobes) co- 
occur in the micro-aerated fermentation, these multiple steps could 
not be readily differentiated. Therefore, model substrates were utilized 
to figure out the role of micro-aeration on each fermentation step. Fig. 3 
(g) presents the influence of different levels of micro-aeration on the 
hydrolysis of BSA (model protein) and dextran (model carbohydrate) on 
day 3. Dextran showed a significantly (two-sample t-test, Welch 
correction, p = 0.003) higher degradation than BSA, suggesting that 
microbes preferred carbohydrate to protein. However, the degradation

3.3. Long-term performance of intermittent micro-aeration anaerobic 
fermentation reactor 
The batch fermentation experiments verified that micro-aeration 
could remarkably enhance the anaerobic fermentation of high-rate 
activated sludge and increase the acetate proportion in fermentate. 
Meanwhile, the intermittent micro-aeration was proved to avoid the 
negative effect caused by the aerobic respiration of facultative anaer­
obes in the later stage. To further evaluate the long-term operation 
performance of CEHRAS fermentation with micro-aeration participa­
tion, one SBR with intermittently micro-aerated anaerobic fermentation 
(MaSBR) was implemented for 30 days. In contrast, another SBR without 
aeration (AnSBR) was also operated for 15 days. Taking into account the 
VFA production, acetate proportion and economic feasibility, the 
optimal operation conditions from batch experiments were adopted into 
the MaSBR and AnSBR, respectively. As summarized on Table 1, the 45 
min/60 min of micro-aeration at 7.69 mL/(L⋅min) had the highest ace­
tate production, though its acetate proportion was lower than the 
continuous micro-aeration at 7.69 mL/(L⋅min). Here, we preliminarily 
believed that the 45 min/60 min of micro-aeration at 7.69 mL/(L⋅min) 
was the optimal condition by considering the power consumption of air 
supply. Thereby, the SRT of MaSBR and AnSBR were 5 days and 2 days, 
respectively. The total intermittent aeration cycle of MaSBR was 60 min 
with an aerated cycle of 45 min. Note that a comprehensive techno- 
economic analysis is needed to evaluate the micro-aeration mode and 
parameters in the future.

facilitate the constitution of syntrophic relationship among microor­
ganisms. It was found that the abundance of some facultative acidogens 
(e.g., Petrimonas, Propioniciclava, and Gemmobacter) and aerobic bacteria 
(e.g., Stenotrophomonas) [29,70–72] in MaSBR were higher than those in 
AnSBR. For instance, Petrimonas, a typical VFA and hydrogen producer 
in fermenters, increased from 1.12% to 3.01% (two-sample t-test, p <
0.001). Li et al. [29] pointed out the abundance of Petrimonas was 
improved after CaO2 addition during WAS anaerobic fermentation. 
CaO2 could slowly release O2, H2O2, and Ca(OH)2, which may facilitate 
the formation of reactive oxygen species, thus a similar micro-aeration 
environment were constructed. Therefore, micro-aeration is conducive 
to establish microbial communities containing higher activity and 
abundance of facultative, strict anaerobic and aerobic bacteria, though 
no obvious distinction in microbial diversity between AnSBR and 
MaSBR. In addition, according to the previous experimental results, 
Erysipelothrix, Tissierella, and Guggenheimella were the three dominant 
genus in CEHRAS fermentation after alkali treatment (pH 10), ac­
counting for 8.97%, 6.88% and 8.38% of the total abundance (Data not 
shown), indicating that the microbial consortia constituted via micro- 
aeration tending to more uniform, enrichment and balance due to 
relative mild-pH condition. 
More importantly, no methanogens were detected in all groups in the 
domain archaea, it is likely that the operational conditions of CEHRAS 
SBR (low HRT and SRT) suppressed the propagation of archaea species, 
which means the VFA consumption steps (methanogenesis) could be 
effectively avoided. Thereby, the CEHRAS exhibited unique advantage 
and potential as a feedstock substrate in anaerobic fermentation. 
3.4. Insights into the application of micro-aerated fermentate for 
heterotrophic denitratation based on model evaluation 
According to the above findings, the micro-aeration treatment has 
satisfying VFA production and acetate proportion, which was obviously 
better than that obtained by strictly anaerobic fermentation. Numerous 
studies have reported that higher nitrite accumulation when acetate 
serves as the carbon source [16–18,73,74]. Accordingly, it could be 
inferred that micro-aerated fermentate could be an ideal carbon source 
for heterotrophic denitrification. We conducted a series of batch deni­
trification experiments using synthetic and real fermentate to verify this 
assumption and developed the dual-substrate and two-step denitrifica­
tion (DSTSN) model (detailed in SI). Based on model fitting and 
parameter estimation, we predicted the influence of the carbon/nitrate 
ratio, acetate proportion in fermentate, and the model parameters on 
heterotrophic denitrification. 
3.4.1. The different nitrite accumulation performance between acetate and 
non-acetate VFA 
As illustrated in Fig. 8(a) ~ (j), the synthetic fermentate without 
acetate exhibited remarkably worse nitrite accumulation than the syn­
thetic fermentate with acetate. At the early stage of the batch experi­
ment, the nitrate reduction rate (0.0848 mg N/L/min) and the nitrite 
accumulation rate (0.0117 mg N/L/min) of the fermentate without ac­
etate were significantly lower (one-sample t-test, p < 0.001) than the 
mean rates of all the synthetic fermentate containing acetate (0.170 and 
0.0622 mg N/L/min, respectively) (Table S4). The VFA profiles during 
denitrification of the real micro-aerated fermentate (Fig. 9) show that 
the acetate consumption rate was much higher than that of other VFA 
components. Furthermore, the nitrite accumulation was almost 
completed in the feast phase of the extracellular carbon source for 
denitrification. In this feast phase of extracellular carbon sources, the 
intracellular storage product formation processes on nitrate (proc 1 and 
proc 2) were dominant in nitrite formation. Meanwhile, intracellular 
storage product formation processes on nitrite (proc 3 and proc 4) were 
the main approaches to consuming nitrite. Thus, the difference between 
the model parameters of the storage processes of SAc and SNAc could 
illuminate the distinction in the nitrite accumulation and the extracel­
lular carbon consumption of the batch experiments. 
As shown in Table S3, the estimated parameter results for synthetic 
fermentate show that the saturation constants of acetate and non-acetate 
(KAc,P1 and KNAc,P2) were 20.2 and 48.9 mg COD/L, respectively, indi­
cating a higher affinity for acetate in the nitrite formation processes 
(proc 1 and 2). Moreover, the storage process rate constant of acetate 
was 2.67 times higher than non-acetate VFAs (qSTO,P1 = 0.738 mg 
CODSTO/L/min, qSTO,P2 = 0.277 mg CODSTO/L/min). The corresponding 
parameters had a similar tendency in the nitrite consumption processes 
(proc 3 and 4). Thus, compared with the non-acetate extracellular car­
bon source, the formation and consumption rates of nitrite and carbon 
source consumption rate were higher when the intracellular storage 
product was converted from acetate. Although the storage process rates 
on nitrate (proc 1 and 2) were lower than that on nitrite (proc 3 and 4), 
the extracellular carbon source saturation constants (KAc,P1 and KNAc,P2) 
of the former processes were much lower than the later corresponding 
constants (KAc,P3 and KNAc,P4). Consequently, the nitrite formation rate 
was higher than the consumption rate during the synthesis phase of the 
intracellular storage product. In this case, both acetate and non-acetate 
VFAs had the nitrite accumulation phenomenon. Furthermore, the rate 
ratio of nitrite formation to consumption using acetate was higher than 
that using non-acetate VFA. Thus, acetate displayed higher nitrite 
accumulation than non-acetate VFA. In a word, the above experimental 
data and model parameter values illustrated that acetate was the key 
VFA in the fermentate of high-rate activated sludge to facilitate nitrite 
accumulation. 
In addition, the peak of internal storage products (XSTO) profiles 
(Fig. 8) increased with the enhancement of the acetate proportion. The 
peak reflects the amount of the suitable substates for the synthesis stage 
of intracellular storage product, i.e., the feast phase of the extracellular 
carbon source, which is the main stage for the nitrite accumulation 
[20,75]. It means the fermentate with higher acetate proportion trig­
gered satisfactory performance in the heterotrophic denitratation pro­
cess, which would be discussed in the following.

proportion, nitrate could be almost entirely depleted during the batch 
experiment cycle. After the nitrate was used up, the remaining extra­
cellular and intracellular carbon sources as electron donors continued to 
support the nitrite reduction, which caused the decrease of nitrite 
accumulation at the later stage of the batch experiments (Fig. 8(d)~(f)).

3.4.3. The start-up and operation of heterotrophic denitratation reactor 
With the parameter values regulated for real fermentate, this study 
simulated the batch experiments of the sludge from different stages of 
the start-up and operation of heterotrophic denitratation reactors. The 
heterotrophic denitratation reactors were fed into different carbon/ni­
trate ratios and acetate proportions of fermentate. To focus on the 
mechanisms and simplify the simulations, assumed that during the 
maturing process of the heterotrophic denitratation sludge, the process 
rate constants of storage and anoxic growth on nitrate were kept un­
changed. In contrast, the corresponding constants on nitrite (i.e., nitrite 
reduction rate (NiR)) were reduced with the running time. 
As illustrated in Fig. 10(a), (d), and (g), when the initial carbon/ni­
trate ratio was 2.0 ~ 3.0 mg COD/mg N (a range which is mostly 
adopted in literature), the time that nitrite accumulation increased to 
80% of the maximum had a negative correlation with acetate propor­
tion. Moreover, this negative relationship was more pronounced as the 
cultivation process continued, suggesting that a higher acetate propor­
tion in the fermentate was more conducive to reduce HRT, reduce the 
reactor size, or increase treatment loading. However, as shown in Fig. 10

COD/mg N, the maximum nitrite accumulation was independent of the 
acetate proportion, which was in accordance with the experimental re­

accumulation had a positive correlation with the initial carbon/nitrite 
ratio, which was consistent with Fig. 8(c) vs. (g), (d) vs. (h), and (f) vs. 
(j). As shown in Fig. 10(c), (f), and (i), the NAR at the time of the

4. Conclusion 
Micro-aeration is an effective technology to enhance VFA production 
and acetate proportion of anaerobic fermentation with CEHRAS as 
substrates. The aeration intensity and cycle time are two crucial factors 
for regulating multiple bioprocesses (i.e., hydrolysis, acidogenesis, 
acetogenesis, and aerobic oxidation) in the micro-aerated fermentation 
of CEHRAS. High intensities of continuous micro-aeration inevitably 
cause high-level aerobic respiration of hydrolyzed and acidified prod­
ucts. The intermittent aeration can effectively limit aerobic oxidation in 
the later fermentation stage. Micro-aeration can enhance the hydrolysis, 
acidogenesis, and acetogenesis steps of proteins, whereas no obvious 
effect on the degradation of carbohydrates. The actual long-term oper­
ation of CEHRAS anaerobic fermentation with micro-aeration assistant 
is feasible and economical. The addition of micro-aerated fermentate 
into the mainstream line of WRRFs has lower increments of nitrogen and 
phosphorus loadings than that of the regular anaerobic fermentate. The 
batch denitrification tests and DSTSN model evaluation disclosed that 
acetate is the crucial component in VFAs to trigger high nitrite accu­
mulation. Higher acetate proportion can shorten the reaction time, in­
crease nitrite accumulation ratio, and extend nitrite accumulation 
duration. Therefore, micro-aerated fermentate is conducive to successful 
denitratation reactor operation, especially in the start-up stage.
